newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont jury to continue deliberations Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont jury to continue deliberations Saturday.

text.p: Jurors in the John du Pont murder trial focused on the definition of first-degree murder as they ended a fourth day of deliberations without a verdict on Friday and prepared to return on Saturday.
Several jurors showed the strain of their drawn-out task as they were dismissed for the day by Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins.
Jenkins kept them on an hour later than normal on Friday evening, and told them to return Saturday, when she said she would answer a late question they posed.
After the dismissal, assistant prosecutor Joe Grace told reporters the jury had asked once again to hear the definition of first-degree murder under Pennsylvania law.
"They want a redefinition of first-degree murder," Grace said.
This would be the fifth time the murder definition would be read to the jurors, including during initial instructions.
The focus of the jurors' questions has steadily narrowed, and Friday's request made no mention of the third-degree murder and voluntary manslaughter charges jurors had previously asked about.
A key issue appeared to be the question of legal malice, the presence of which is required, along with premeditation, for a conviction of first-degree murder.

The jurors have heard repeated definitions of legal malice, which Jenkins described as an intent to kill or cause serious bodily injury, or extreme indifference to human life. Third-degree murder implies malice, but no intent to kill.
Du Pont, a millionaire chemicals heir, is charged with first and third-degree murder as well as voluntary manslaughter in the Jan. 26, 1996 killing of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
Du Pont's lawyers have conceded du Pont killed Schultz, and are seeking a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity, saying he was unaware of the wrongfulness of his acts.
In addition to verdicts of not guilty, or not guilty by reason of insanity, the jurors can render verdicts of guilty or guilty but mentally ill.
